additional_requirements: Functioning is not markedly impaired apart from the impact of the delusion(s) or its ramifications

S019.name: Delusions
S019.description: Fixed beliefs that do not change easily, even in the face of contradictory evidence.

subtypes.Persecutory Delusions: The false belief that one is being harmed or monitored by other people or organizations.
subtypes.Referential Delusions: The conviction that ordinary events, remarks, or behaviors have specific relevance to oneself.
subtypes.Grandiose Delusions: The false belief that one possesses special abilities, power, or fame.
subtypes.Erotomanic Delusions: The false belief that another person is in love with or has affection for them.
subtypes.Nihilistic Delusions: A destructive or negative conviction that the world is ending or that a major catastrophe will occur.
subtypes.Somatic Delusions: The baseless conviction that there is a serious abnormality with one's body or organs.
subtypes.Jealous Delusions: The conviction that one's spouse or romantic partner is being unfaithful without sufficient evidence.

symptom.disease_info: Delusional disorder is characterized by one or more non-bizarre or less obviously bizarre delusions lasting at least one month, in the absence of prominent hallucinations, disorganized thought, or marked mood episodes that would suggest schizophrenia or a primary mood disorder with psychotic features. Outside of the delusional beliefs, functioning can be relatively preserved, and behavior often appears normal unless directly influenced by the delusional system. Onset is typically in mid to late adulthood and the course is often chronic, with beliefs remaining fixed despite clear contradictory evidence and limited insight. Subtypes may center on themes such as persecution, jealousy, erotomania, or somatic concerns, and clinicians distinguish delusional disorder from culturally sanctioned beliefs by assessing idiosyncrasy, rigidity, and the degree of functional impairment or interpersonal conflict produced by the delusions.

patient.stressor: Around eighteen months ago, as Loretta’s adult children became more independent and she shifted her energy into choir, community walking groups, and her new home-organization consulting work, she began to fixate on subtle changes in her husband’s routines and interactions at church. What started as occasional suspicion during choir practice planning meetings gradually solidified over the next year into an unshakable conviction about his supposed hidden activities, despite consistent reassurance from family and friends and no corroborating evidence. Her growing preoccupation with these beliefs began to intrude on her quilting circles and seniors walking group, where she started questioning others’ motives and declining invitations tied to her husband’s social network. The situation came to clinical attention when marital counseling with their pastor stalled over her inability to reconsider her beliefs, and the pastor, concerned about how entrenched they had become despite minimal other changes in her functioning, encouraged a psychiatric evaluation.
patient.chief_complaint: “I know everyone keeps telling me I’m wrong, but I’m absolutely certain about what my husband is hiding from me, and nothing they say changes my mind.”

S019.name: Delusions
S019.description: Fixed beliefs that do not change easily, even in the face of contradictory evidence.
S019.manifestation: Ever since I started noticing little things—him lingering after choir meetings, changing his phone password, whispering with that younger woman from church—I’ve just known in my gut that he’s sneaking around on me and hiding some kind of affair, and no matter how many times he swears he isn’t and the kids tell me I’m overreacting, I can’t shake the certainty that they’re all covering for him.

add_requirements.Functioning is not markedly impaired apa: Outside of this whole situation with my husband, I still keep up with my housework, go to choir practice, and run my little home-organization jobs just fine, and people at church say I seem like my usual self unless the topic of my husband and that woman comes up.
add_requirements.functional_impairment: I’ve stopped going to some choir gatherings and walking group outings if I think my husband or that woman might be there, and it’s caused so many fights at home that the kids visit less because they’re tired of hearing me bring it up.
add_requirements.duration: It’s been a little over a year now—since about last spring—that I’ve been convinced my husband is hiding this from me and I haven’t been able to let it go.
